title: Native-Like Use of Modality and Attitude
subtitle: C2 modality goes beyond certainty/possibility to convey fine shades of tentativeness, concession, politeness and layered epistemic stance — how confident, cauti…
objectives: Understand and use: Subtle modal shading

Understand and use: Layered modality — combining more than one modal expression (typically a modal + a modal-like verb phrase such as "expected to," "supposed to," "meant to") to express a nuanced, sometimes ironic, stance on an obligation or expectation that itself involves uncertainty.
Understand and use: Epistemic stance markers — phrases that signal how the writer/speaker is framing their own certainty, common in academic and diplomatic register.

content.intro: C2 modality goes beyond certainty/possibility to convey fine shades of tentativeness, concession, politeness and layered epistemic stance — how confident, cautious or diplomatic the speaker wants to sound.

rules.heading: a) Subtle modal shading
rules.body:
• Tentativeness/hedging: might, could, would seem to, it could be said that, one might argue. It would seem that the strategy has largely failed. (softer, more diplomatic than "The strategy has failed")
  • Concession within modality: may/might + well (acknowledging a point is likely true, often before contrasting it): She might well be right, but I still have reservations.
  • Politeness distancing: would/could/might used to soften requests, suggestions or opinions, creating social distance and respect. Might I suggest an alternative approach? (very formal/polite) vs. Can I suggest...? (neutral)

rules.heading: b) Layered modality — combining more than one modal expression (typically a modal + a modal-like verb phrase such as "expected to," "supposed to," "meant to") to express a nuanced, sometimes ironic, stance on an obligation or expectation that itself involves uncertainty.
rules.body:
He might have been expected to apologize, but he never did. (= it would have been reasonable to expect an apology, though uncertainty/distance is baked in)

She should, in theory, have been informed beforehand.

rules.heading: c) Epistemic stance markers — phrases that signal how the writer/speaker is framing their own certainty, common in academic and diplomatic register.
rules.body:
It is conceivable that... / There is reason to believe that... / One cannot rule out the possibility that... / It stands to reason that...

Native-like control means choosing the modal combination that matches exactly how certain, cautious, or polite you intend to sound — not just whether something is possible or necessary.

examples: It would seem that the negotiations have reached a stalemate.
She might well be the most qualified candidate, but the panel remains divided.
Might I suggest we revisit this proposal at a later date?
He might have been expected to resign after the scandal, yet he remains in office.
One cannot rule out the possibility that the results were affected by bias.
There is reason to believe that the original estimate was overly optimistic.
It could be argued that the reform, while well-intentioned, was poorly executed.
She should, in theory, have received the documents by now.
It stands to reason that costs would rise given the current shortages.
He may well have a point, but the timing of his objection is questionable.

commonMistakes.wrong: It would seem the strategy fails.
commonMistakes.right: It would seem that the strategy has failed.
commonMistakes.why: This hedged structure typically requires "that" before the clause, and the verb tense should match the intended time frame (here, a completed failure).
After "might well," use the bare infinitive ("be"), not the gerund.

commonMistakes.wrong: He might have expected to apologize.
commonMistakes.right: He might have been expected to apologize.
commonMistakes.why: "Be expected to" is a passive structure (others expected it of him); dropping "been" changes the meaning to "he expected himself."

commonMistakes.wrong: It cannot rule out the possibility that costs will rise.
commonMistakes.right: One cannot rule out the possibility that costs will rise.
commonMistakes.why: The impersonal subject here is "one" (or "we"), not "it" — "it" doesn't fit this fixed epistemic phrase.

commonMistakes.wrong: Might I to suggest an alternative?
commonMistakes.why: After the inverted modal "Might I," use the bare infinitive directly, without "to."

exercises.title: Gap-fill
exercises.instructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correct modal/epistemic phrase)

items.prompt: It would ___ (seem) that the plan has stalled entirely.
items.explanation: “It would seem that” is the fixed hedging frame — “seem” completes it.

items.prompt: She might ___ (well) be correct, but I'd like more evidence.
items.explanation: “Might well” concedes a point is likely true before a contrast.

items.prompt: ___ I suggest we postpone the decision until next week? (very formal request)
items.explanation: Inverted “Might I…?” is the very formal/polite way to make a suggestion.

items.prompt: He ___ (might/expect) to know better, given his experience.
items.explanation: “Might have been expected to” (passive) shows others expected it of him, with a layer of uncertainty.

items.prompt: There is reason ___ (believe) the figures were manipulated.
items.explanation: “There is reason to” + bare infinitive is the fixed epistemic frame.

items.prompt: It ___ (stand/reason) that demand would fall as prices rose.
items.explanation: “It stands to reason that” is the fixed idiom for a logical inference.

items.prompt: One cannot ___ (rule out) the possibility of further delays.
items.explanation: “Cannot rule out” is the fixed phrase for an epistemic possibility that can't be excluded.

items.prompt: She should, in theory, ___ (already/inform) of the changes.
items.explanation: The passive perfect (“have been informed”) shows the informing was done by someone else, by now.

exercises.title: Rewrite / Transformation
exercises.instructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each direct statement with the appropriate hedged/modal tone)

items.prompt: The results are wrong. (make it tentative/hedged)
answer: It would seem that the results are incorrect.
items.explanation: “It would seem that” softens the direct claim into a hedge.

items.prompt: Costs will definitely rise. (make it a cautious epistemic claim, not a certainty)
answer: There is reason to believe that costs will rise.
items.explanation: “There is reason to believe that” turns the certainty into a cautious epistemic claim.

items.prompt: Can I suggest a different approach? (make it more formal/polite)
answer: Might I suggest a different approach?
items.explanation: Inverted “Might I…?” is more formal/polite than “Can I…?”

items.prompt: He should have apologized. (add a layer of distance — "might have been expected to")
answer: He might have been expected to apologize.
items.explanation: “Might have been expected to” adds a layer of distance/uncertainty to the obligation.

items.prompt: Bias affected the results. (rewrite as a possibility that can't be excluded, using "one cannot rule out...")
answer: One cannot rule out the possibility that bias affected the results.
items.explanation: “One cannot rule out the possibility that” reframes the claim as an unexcluded possibility.

items.incorrect: It would seem the negotiations collapse.
answer: It would seem that the negotiations have collapsed.
items.explanation: This hedged structure needs “that” before the clause, with the verb tense matching the intended time frame.

items.incorrect: She might well being the best candidate.
answer: She might well be the best candidate.
items.explanation: After “might well,” use the bare infinitive (“be”), not the gerund.

items.incorrect: He might have expect an apology from her.
answer: He might have expected an apology from her.
items.explanation: “Be expected to” is a passive structure — dropping “been” changes the meaning to “he expected himself.”

items.incorrect: It cannot rule out the possibility of a delay.
answer: One cannot rule out the possibility of a delay.
items.explanation: The impersonal subject in this fixed epistemic phrase is “one,” not “it.”

items.incorrect: Might I to ask a question?
items.explanation: After the inverted modal “Might I,” use the bare infinitive directly, without “to.”

items.incorrect: There is reason believe the data is flawed.
answer: There is reason to believe the data is flawed.
items.explanation: “There is reason” is followed by “to” + bare infinitive: reason to believe.

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using "It would seem that..." to hedge an opinion about current events.
items.modelAnswer: It would seem that remote work has permanently changed employer expectations.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using "might well" to concede a point before disagreeing with it.
items.modelAnswer: He might well be telling the truth, but I still think we should verify his story.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using "One cannot rule out the possibility that..." about an uncertain outcome.
items.modelAnswer: One cannot rule out the possibility that the delay will affect the entire launch schedule.

items.prompt: Write one very formal, polite request using inverted "Might I...?"
items.modelAnswer: Might I ask you to reconsider your decision before the meeting concludes?

summary: b) Layered modality — combining more than one modal expression (typically a modal + a modal-like verb phrase such as "expected to," "supposed to," "meant to") to express a nuanced, sometimes ironic, stance on an obligation or expectation that itself involves uncertainty.
c) Epistemic stance markers — phrases that signal how the writer/speaker is framing their own certainty, common in academic and diplomatic register.
